Cliff swallows (Petrochelidon pyrrhonota) typically construct their gourd-shaped mud nests in large, dense colonies under bridges, overpasses, and on cliff faces throughout much of North America. During the early stages of development, nestlings exhibit a striking growth trajectory, with freshly hatched chicks having an initial wet weight of just 2.1 grams [Ww0 = 2.1 grams]. Field studies have demonstrated that the typical age at hatching for this species is 14 days [ab = 14 days] under incubation temperatures of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a developmental period that aligns well with that of other aerially insectivorous hirundines. The precise thermal conditions of the nest during incubation are critical, as even minor deviations from this standard can significantly impact hatching success and the subsequent health of the altricial nestlings. Colony density itself creates a unique microclimate, with the cumulative body heat of brooding adults helping to maintain stable temperatures within the mud chambers.

Once hatched, the cliff swallow nestling must undergo a rapid phase of somatic growth before it can achieve independence. The wet weight at birth for these chicks is consistently recorded at 1.9 grams [Wwb = 1.9 grams], a value that reflects the substantial maternal investment in egg yolk provisioned by the female. Under the active metabolic temperatures characteristic of a thriving colony, which hover around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging occurs approximately 25 days after hatching [tx = approximately 25 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone is preceded by an observable peak in growth rate, during which the pin-feathered chick transforms into a fully feathered juvenile. The timing of nest departure is critical, as it must coincide with peak insect abundance to ensure the newly fledged bird can successfully feed itself. Parents continue to provision the fledgling for a short period, gradually reducing feedings to encourage nutritional independence.

Reproductive output in cliff swallows shows considerable plasticity in response to local environmental conditions. When measured at the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 75 days [tp = 75 days]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity allows for a compressed breeding cycle in the short temperate summer. Females typically lay between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch], with the clutch size showing notable year-to-year variation linked to the availability of flying insects. The species is capable of producing approximately 1.25 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.25 clutches per year], a strategy that maximizes reproductive output when conditions are favorable. Some pairs in high-quality habitats may initiate a second brood immediately after the first fledges, whereas those in poorer areas may only successfully rear a single brood.

Longevity and first reproduction in Petrochelidon pyrrhonota are heavily influenced by the high costs of colonial living, including intense competition for nest sites and high parasite loads. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, under the active thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], is approximately 11.8 years [am = approximately 11.8 years]. This is a relatively extended lifespan for a small passerine, suggesting a conservative life-history strategy once adulthood is reached. Furthermore, the time since birth at first brood for cliff swallows is typically one year (1 year since birth) [tR = 1 year since birth], meaning that most individuals do not begin breeding until the spring following their birth year at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay likely allows young birds to accumulate sufficient foraging experience and somatic reserves to successfully compete for a nest site within the highly structured hierarchy of a dense colony.

The asymptotic wet weight of a nestling cliff swallow, representing the maximum body mass achieved before fledging, has been measured at 26.6 grams [Wwi = 26.6 grams]. This value is notable because it typically exceeds the average mass of an adult bird, which often weighs less due to the energetic demands of sustained flight and foraging. The growth curve that leads to this peak mass is sigmoidal, with the most rapid gains occurring between days five and fifteen post-hatching. Such a strategy is energetically expensive for the provisioning parents, which must make thousands of foraging trips over the nestling period to collect enough insect prey to satisfy the growing brood. Compared to other hirundines of similar body size, the cliff swallow's peak nestling mass reflects a relatively high investment in offspring quality, likely an adaptation to the intense competition for nest sites within dense colonies.
